verdict.reason: Both debates converge on the same sound plan (pause, settle, reintroduce singly, with a medical exit ramp), but A's objections do more work: the combination problem, the weakness of forearm patch tests for facial skin, and the need to define in advance what counts as a reaction each change the method rather than restate it. B's distinctive move is a motive-reading of the user that it then contests and turns into a useful branch, but it leaves the patch test and the stacked-actives possibility unexamined.

comparisons.a_observation: The Subtractor raises that products may be fine singly and harsh together, so single reintroduction could acquit every product; later it attacks the Experimenter's forearm patch test (facial skin reacts differently) and the risk of restarting the clock, and the Experimenter explicitly concedes the slower trial while holding the line on reintroduction.
comparisons.b_observation: The retest-too-soon objection narrows the Experimenter's claim to a clean baseline, and the Skeptic adds a replication point, but the Experimenter's own patch-test proposal goes unchallenged and no one considers interaction between products.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Three products started at once is exactly the case where a stacked combination can be the cause and where a weak patch test can mislead, so A's objections change what the user would actually do (test pairs if singles are clean; do not trust the forearm alone).

comparisons.a_observation: Turns the vague word 'sting' into a measurement problem: decide beforehand what counts (lasting redness, burning after rinsing, flaking) and log at ten minutes and an hour; dependsOn offers dropping a non-essential product as a legitimate cheaper path.
comparisons.b_observation: Offers a speculative reading of the user's motives, which the Subtractor contests from the user's actual wording, and the Experimenter converts the two readings into different advice (rescue products vs. just get comfortable).
comparisons.why_it_matters: A sharpens the user's 'figure out what's causing it' into observable criteria; B ties the depth of investigation to what the user wants, which is also decision-relevant. Each helps on a different axis.

comparisons.a_observation: Branches on fading vs. not fading, other changes that week, red-flag symptoms, and whether a product is essential; reintroduce one every one to two weeks.
comparisons.b_observation: Branches on severity (including trouble breathing), mild and fading, comfort-only goals, and adds that a sting not easing after a week or two of a minimal routine warrants a dermatologist.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both give the user observable conditions; B's persistent-sting-to-dermatologist branch and A's combination-testing branch are each a real addition the other lacks.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[4].text: The point that single-product retesting can acquit every product while the combination (e.g. two layered exfoliating acids) is the cause, with the concrete fix of testing pairs if singles come back clean.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[7].text: The Experimenter turns the contested reading of the user's motives into a branch: a slow test is worth it if the user wants to rescue products, poor value if they only want comfort, with the clinician exit applying to both.

concerns.description: Speculates about the user's hopes and fears about the products without basis in the input; it is labelled as rejectable and contested in the next turn, so the effect is limited.
Recommends a forearm or behind-the-ear patch test as the first step without noting that facial skin may react differently, which could give false reassurance.
Red-flag list omits breathing difficulty as an urgent-care trigger and draws no urgency distinction between seeing a doctor or pharmacist and emergency care.
